title_original: The Book Column : Elsa Martinez & Marie Hervé : Que le feu soit tendre, que la mer soit bonne
excerpt_original: Publié chez Cé Éditions, les photographes Elsa Martinez et Marie Hervé explorent dans 'Que le feu soit tendre, que la mer soit bonne' les mythes et les fractures de la Méditerranée entre vestiges de l'Antiquité et monde contemporain. Cet article The Book Column : Elsa Martinez &…

blocks.text: In Que le feu soit tendre, que la mer soit bonne , published by C é É ditions, photographers Elsa Martinez and Marie Herv é explore the myths and fractures of the Mediterranean through a distinctive form of archaeology, in which remnants of antiquity stand alongside those of our contemporary world.

Could a column by the side of a road hold as much value as the Winged Victory of Samothrace? For Elsa Martinez and Marie Hervé, the question is worth asking. For the past six years, the two French photographers have travelled across the Mediterranean, exploring its museums, ruins and landscapes in search of traces left by ancient civilisations and our own era. In their first collaboratively authored monograph, Que le feu soit tendre, que la mer soit bonne , they propose an archaeology freed from hierarchies and chronologies, where past and present seem to merge.

Their collaboration began while studying at the École nationale supérieure de la photographie in Arles, brought together by a shared interest in the Mediterranean, rooted in their respective family histories. In 2020, they embarked on their first exploration of Sicily, followed by further journeys to Puglia, Greece and Palestine, gradually building a vast photographic archive over the years.

Setting out to explore this mythologised territory, regarded as the cradle of Western civilisation, the two artists gradually uncovered its contradictions. Behind the remnants of a glorious past emerge the fractures of a contemporary world marked by inequality, power imbalances and conflict. As their research progresses, historical and geographical certainties begin to falter. “What do we keep, and what do we discard?” they ask, confronted with the sense of a world slowly crumbling.

This reflection runs through the photographs in the book, where fragments of ancient sculptures, religious objects and ruins enter into dialogue with volcanic landscapes, urban views, fragments of the human body and remnants of the everyday. Materials echo one another: stone, flesh, earth, bone, marble. Moving between black and white and colour, from minute details to the vastness of the landscape, the images constantly blur scales and temporal boundaries. The real sits alongside the fake, ancient artefacts alongside contemporary objects. Through this speculative archaeology, the photographers question both the value we assign to things and the narratives we construct around them.

Conceived as an extension of their artistic practice, the book embraces this same freedom. Without captions, page numbers or chronological progression, the photographs form an imaginary map in which places and eras intertwine. Images unfold through associations of shapes, materials and motifs, in a rhythm of returns and repetitions. Some sequences delve deep into the surfaces of rocks, until the landscape dissolves into abstraction. Others are punctuated by monochromatic images printed in silver ink, derived from the artists’ screen prints on concrete. Resembling stelae, they punctuate the book and lend it a distinctive material quality.

At the heart of this exploration lies a text by writer Théo Casciani, a futuristic fable in which the Mediterranean itself seems destined to dissolve. Rather than explaining the photographs, the narrative extends their speculative dimension. Its typography reinforces this movement: silver lettering gradually takes precedence over black, as though the text were disintegrating before our eyes. Photography, writing and printed matter thus merge into a shared reflection on the fragility of things and their potential disappearance.

Refusing to impose a fixed meaning on their images, Elsa Martinez and Marie Hervé leave readers free to make their own associations. Que le feu soit tendre, que la mer soit bonne does not seek to compile an inventory of the Mediterranean, still less to offer a definitive account of its history. Instead, it turns uncertainty into a space for creation, where remnants become fragments of a story waiting to be reinvented. And it invites us to see ruins not merely as witnesses to a bygone past, but as living traces of our present.
Elsa Martinez & Marie Hervé — Que le feu soit tendre, que la mer soit bonne Published by Cé Éditions, 2026 Text by Théo Casciani 178 pages, 20.5 × 29 cm
